why_how.text: Shapes can be read from far away or when words are hidden, so each shape carries its own meaning.
The pennant is a special warning shape for no-passing zones, separate from the general diamond.
Two different shapes both mean a railroad crossing, so either one tells you to look for trains.
Rectangles split by direction: a wide one gives directions and a tall one states a law.

scenario.text: Jo sees a five-sided sign far ahead, too far away to read.

reasoning.text: A diamond marks a warning sign, and a five-sided pentagon marks a school sign.

result.text: Jo slows and watches for children, knowing a school sign is ahead.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating the pennant as just another diamond warning sign.

correction.text: The pennant shape is tied to no-passing zones, while the diamond is the general warning shape.

prompt.text: A tall, vertical rectangle sign stands beside the road. What kind of message does it usually carry?

rationale.text: A horizontal rectangle gives directions, while a vertical rectangle states a law.

narration.text: This lesson is about reading signs by their shape. A sign's shape hints at its meaning, and the handbook teaches nine basic shapes to recognize. That matters because you often see a sign's outline long before you can read its words, and sometimes snow, dirt or glare hides the words entirely. We will go through the octagon, triangle, diamond, pentagon, pennant, the two rectangles, the round sign and the crossbuck. Practice questions often show a shape or describe it and ask what it means, so the goal is to link each outline to its message right away.

The eight-sided octagon means STOP, and the triangle means YIELD. These two are so important that their shapes are used for nothing else. A diamond shape marks a warning sign, telling you about a hazard or change ahead. A five-sided pentagon marks a school sign, warning that you are near a school or a school crossing. So four shapes give you four different messages: stop, yield, take care, and watch for children. Picture each outline as you say its meaning. The octagon has the most sides, and it asks the most of you: a complete stop.

A pennant shape warns of a no-passing zone. It is long and pointed, like a flag lying on its side. Rectangles come in two directions. A horizontal rectangle gives directions, such as which way to go to reach a town. A vertical rectangle states a law, such as a speed limit or a turn rule. So a wide sign usually guides you, and a tall sign usually tells you what the law requires. That simple split helps when you are scanning a busy roadside, because you can tell at a glance whether a sign is giving advice about the route or setting a rule you must follow.

Both the round sign and the crossbuck mean a railroad crossing. The round sign usually comes first, as an advance warning that a crossing is ahead. The crossbuck, shaped like a large X, stands at the crossing itself. Two different shapes, one meaning: either one tells you to look for trains. This is the only meaning in the set that uses two shapes, which is why it is worth remembering on its own. When you see either shape, slow down, look both ways, and be ready to stop. The shape is the cue, and the right response is the same for both.

lines.text: Trap: a pennant is just a warning.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The pennant shape is tied to no-passing zones, while the diamond is the general warning shape. Both are warning signs in a broad sense, but the pennant has one specific job. Options may say the pennant warns of curves or schools, or that a diamond means no passing. Both are wrong. Curves and other hazards use diamonds. Schools use the pentagon. And no passing uses the pennant. When a question describes a long, pointed sign, think no passing. When it describes a square turned on its corner, think general warning ahead.

Here is a quick check: a tall, vertical rectangle sign stands beside the road ahead. What kind of message does it usually carry? Recall the two rectangles. A horizontal rectangle gives directions, while a vertical rectangle states a law. This sign is tall, so the answer is a law, such as a speed limit or a turn rule. If the same sign were wide instead of tall, it would usually be giving directions. Reading the shape first lets you prepare to obey before you can even make out the words, which is exactly why shapes are so useful on the road.

lines.text: Pennant no passing; two railroad shapes.

narration.text: To finish, a sign's shape hints at its meaning, and there are nine basic shapes to learn. The octagon means STOP and the triangle means YIELD. The diamond marks a warning and the pentagon marks a school. The pennant warns of a no-passing zone. A horizontal rectangle gives directions, and a vertical rectangle states a law. Both the round sign and the crossbuck mean a railroad crossing, so either one means look for trains. The hook is shape hints the meaning, and the habit is to read the outline first, then the words once you are close enough.

why_how.text: Colors can be recognized before shapes or words, so each one signals a kind of message.
Different caution colors separate general warnings from work zones and incidents.
Information colors tell you what is nearby: services, directions or recreation.

scenario.text: Tom sees a bright pink sign on the freeway one morning.

reasoning.text: Fluorescent pink marks an incident, emergency or unplanned event, unlike orange, which is for planned construction.

result.text: Tom slows and follows the signs that guide traffic around the incident.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking yellow and orange signs mean the same caution.

correction.text: Yellow is the general caution color, but orange is reserved for construction or maintenance, and fluorescent pink is for incidents.

prompt.text: You are looking for a place to eat and get gas. Which sign color should you watch for?

rationale.text: Blue signs point to services and hospitality, while green gives directions and brown points to recreation.

narration.text: This lesson is about sign colors. Like shapes, colors give you a quick read on a sign's message before you can see the words. Some colors set rules, some warn, and some give information about what is nearby. We will go through red, black and white, yellow, orange, the two fluorescent colors, blue, green and brown, and we will see what regulatory signs usually look like. Practice questions often describe a color and ask what it means, or ask which color is used for a certain kind of sign. Grouping the colors by job makes them easier to keep straight.

Red on a sign means stop, prohibited or forbidden. Black and white signs are regulatory, telling you what is legally allowed or prohibited. Regulatory signs set specific laws on traffic speed and movement, and they are usually rectangles in white and black, red, white and black, or red and white. So when you see red, white and black together on a rectangle, you are almost always looking at a law. A speed limit sign is a good example. These are the signs you must obey, not just consider. Red tends to mark the strongest commands, like stop or do not enter.

Yellow signs give caution or a general warning, such as a curve or an intersection ahead. Orange signals caution for construction or maintenance. Fluorescent yellow-green warns of schools, pedestrians or bicycles, so it marks places where people outside cars are likely. Fluorescent pink marks an incident, emergency or unplanned event, such as a crash that has blocked the road. So there are four caution colors, each for a different kind of hazard. Yellow is the everyday warning. The other three point to work zones, vulnerable road users, and sudden trouble on the road.

Blue signs point to services and hospitality, such as gas, food, lodging and hospitals. Green signs give directions and guidance, such as exits, distances and the names of towns. Brown signs point out places of recreation or cultural interest, such as parks, campgrounds and historic sites. These three colors do not give orders or warnings. They tell you what is nearby and how to reach it. If you are lost, look for green. If you need a break or fuel, look for blue. If you are looking for something to see or do, look for brown.

lines.text: Trap: yellow and orange are the same.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Yellow is the general caution color, but orange is caution reserved for construction or maintenance, and fluorescent pink is for incidents and unplanned events. Options may say an orange sign warns of a sharp curve, or that pink marks planned road work. Both are wrong. Curves and everyday hazards use yellow. Planned work uses orange. Sudden events like crashes use pink. The difference matters because each one sets up a different kind of hazard ahead. Orange means workers and equipment. Pink means a situation that was not planned and may still be changing.

Here is a quick check: you are on a long drive and want to find a place to eat and get gas. Which sign color should you watch for? Recall the information colors. Blue signs point to services and hospitality, green signs give directions and guidance, and brown signs point out places of recreation or cultural interest. Food and gas are services, so the answer is blue. A green sign might tell you how far the next town is, and a brown sign might point to a state park, but the blue sign is the one that lists the services you need.

lines.text: Red forbids; black and white regulate.

narration.text: To finish, red means stop, prohibited or forbidden, and black and white signs are regulatory, telling you what is legally allowed or prohibited. Regulatory signs set laws on speed and movement and are usually rectangles in those colors. Yellow gives general caution, orange is for construction or maintenance, fluorescent yellow-green warns of schools, pedestrians or bicycles, and fluorescent pink marks incidents and unplanned events. Blue points to services, green gives directions, and brown points out recreation or culture. The hook is yellow warns, orange works.

why_how.text: Route markers and guide signs help you find your way without stopping to check a map.
Service and parking signs tell you where you may stop and for how long.
An Incident Ahead sign starts a set of signs that lead you around unplanned trouble.

scenario.text: Sam wants to reach a nearby town and sees a green sign naming it with an arrow.

reasoning.text: A destination guide sign tells you which way to go to reach the communities it names.

result.text: Sam follows the arrow toward the town.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an Incident Ahead sign announces planned road work.

correction.text: An Incident Ahead sign means an emergency or unplanned event has disrupted traffic, and the signs after it guide you around or through.

prompt.text: A parking sign allows two-hour parking during the day. What does that tell you?

answer.text: You may park there, but only for a limited time during those hours.

rationale.text: A parking permitted sign can limit how long you stay during set hours.

narration.text: This lesson covers guide and information signs. These signs help you find your way and find what you need: route markers that name the road you are on, destination signs that point to towns, service signs for gas and exits, rest area and school crossing signs, parking signs, and the Incident Ahead sign that warns of unplanned trouble. Most of these signs do not give orders, but reading them correctly keeps you from wrong turns, sudden lane changes and parking tickets. Practice questions often show one of these signs and ask what it tells you, so we will connect each to its message.

lines.text: Route markers name the road system.
State markers, such as M routes.

narration.text: Route markers identify the federal, state and county road systems: interstate freeway, U.S. highway, state highway and county route signs. Each system has its own marker, so you can tell what kind of road you are on at a glance. A state route marker identifies a state highway, such as one of Michigan's M routes. A destination guide sign, such as one naming Brookfield and Onondaga, tells you which way to go to reach those communities. Together, route markers tell you which road you are on, and destination signs tell you which way to turn to reach where you want to go.

A gas pump sign shows where gas stations are, and an Exit sign shows where the freeway exit is. A Rest Area sign points to public restrooms. A School Crossing sign warns of a crossing for children ahead. These are among the most common signs on a trip. The service signs help you plan stops before you reach them, so you can move to the correct lane in good time instead of swerving at the last moment. The School Crossing sign is different. It is a warning, and it asks you to slow down and watch for children as you approach.

lines.text: Incident Ahead: follow the detour signs.

narration.text: A parking sign with a wheelchair symbol reserves the space for people with disabilities. A parking permitted sign can limit the stay, such as two-hour parking during set daytime hours. Read these signs closely, because a space can be legal at one time and a ticket at another. An Incident Ahead sign means an emergency or other unplanned event has disrupted traffic. The signs that follow it guide you around or through the area. So when you see an Incident Ahead sign, slow down, expect changes, and follow the signs that come next rather than guessing at a route.

lines.text: Trap: Incident Ahead means road work.

narration.text: Here is the trap. An Incident Ahead sign means an emergency or other unplanned event has disrupted traffic, and the signs that follow guide you around or through the area. Options may describe it as a sign for planned construction, or claim it means the road is closed for good. Both are wrong. Planned work is announced with orange road work signs. An incident is sudden and unplanned, like a crash. And the road is not simply closed. The signs after the incident sign show you how to get around it. Follow them, and expect the situation to change as you get closer.

Here is a quick check: a parking sign allows two-hour parking during the day. What does that tell you? Recall the parking permitted sign. A parking permitted sign can limit the stay, such as two-hour parking during set daytime hours. So you may park there, but only for a limited time during those hours. Staying longer than the limit during those hours breaks the rule. Outside those hours, the sign itself shows when the limit applies. Reading every line of a parking sign, including the times, is the simplest way to avoid a ticket.

lines.text: Read parking times; follow incident signs.

narration.text: To finish, route markers identify the federal, state and county road systems, and a state route marker identifies a state highway. A destination guide sign tells you which way to go to reach the communities it names. A gas pump sign shows where gas stations are, an Exit sign shows the freeway exit, a Rest Area sign points to restrooms, and a School Crossing sign warns of a children's crossing ahead. A wheelchair parking sign reserves a space for people with disabilities, and a parking permitted sign can limit your stay. An Incident Ahead sign means follow the signs that guide you around unplanned trouble.

why_how.text: Stop and yield signs decide who goes first, so each one asks for a different action.
Advance warning signs give you time to prepare for a stop, yield or roundabout ahead.
Turn and lane-use signs tell you where turns are allowed, so you can choose your lane early.

scenario.text: At a quiet corner, Lee reaches a red octagon and sees no traffic at all.

reasoning.text: At a stop sign, stop completely and yield to traffic and pedestrians before going on.

result.text: Lee comes to a full stop, checks for traffic and pedestrians, and then goes.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a yield sign like a stop sign, or a stop sign like a yield sign.

correction.text: A stop sign requires a complete stop every time; a yield sign requires slowing and letting crossing vehicles go first.

prompt.text: The light is red and a No Turn On Red sign is posted where you want to turn right. What do you do?

answer.text: Wait for the light to change before turning.

rationale.text: No Turn On Red forbids turning on a red light.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs that control what you do at intersections and along the road: stop and yield signs, the advance warnings that come before them, turn restrictions, lane-use signs, one-way signs and speed limit signs. These are regulatory signs, which means they set the law, not just give advice. Practice questions often test the difference between stopping and yielding, and the meaning of turn restrictions. If you can say exactly what each sign requires, you will answer those questions correctly and drive through intersections with fewer surprises for you and for everyone around you.

lines.text: Stop sign: stop completely, then yield.
Yield sign: slow, let crossing traffic go.

narration.text: At a stop sign, stop completely and yield to traffic and pedestrians before going on. At a yield sign, slow down and let vehicles crossing your path go first. The difference is the stop. A stop sign always requires a complete stop, even when the road looks empty. A yield sign requires a stop only when crossing traffic makes it necessary. Roundabout Ahead, Stop Ahead and Yield Ahead signs warn that a roundabout, a stop sign or a yield sign is coming up. They give you time to slow down smoothly, especially where a curve or hill hides the sign until late.

No Turn On Red forbids turning on a red light. Separate signs prohibit right turns or U-turns, whatever the light shows. Lane-use signs show which lanes may turn left, and a Center Lane Left Turn Only sign reserves the middle lane for left turns. These signs are posted where turns would be unsafe or where lanes have special jobs. Read them early, so you can be in the right lane before the intersection. A driver who notices a left-turn-only lane too late may make a sudden lane change, which is exactly the kind of move these signs are meant to prevent.

lines.text: One Way: every lane, same direction.
Speed Limit fifty: the legal maximum.

narration.text: A One Way sign means traffic in every lane moves in the same direction. So on a one-way street, all lanes flow the same way, and turning into it from the wrong end puts you against traffic. A Speed Limit fifty sign sets the legal maximum on that stretch at fifty miles per hour. A speed limit is a law, not a suggestion, and it is the most you may drive under good conditions. Both of these signs are regulatory, which is why they share the rectangle shape and black and white colors. When you see them, the message is what the law requires on this road.

lines.text: Trap: a stop sign means slow down.
Stop sign: complete stop every time.
Yield sign: slow and let others go.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A stop sign and a yield sign ask for different things. At a stop sign, stop completely and yield to traffic and pedestrians before going on. At a yield sign, slow down and let vehicles crossing your path go first. Options may describe rolling slowly through a stop sign when the road is clear, or coming to a full stop at every yield sign as if it were required. The first is wrong, because a stop sign always requires a full stop. A yield sign asks you to slow and give way, and to stop only if crossing traffic makes it necessary.

lines.text: No Turn On Red is posted.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: the light is red, you want to turn right, and a No Turn On Red sign is posted at the corner. What do you do? Recall what the sign forbids. No Turn On Red forbids turning on a red light. So the answer is to wait until the light turns green before making your right turn. Without that sign, a right turn on red may be allowed after a full stop, but the sign removes that option at this corner. These signs are often placed where drivers turning on red would face hidden traffic or heavy pedestrian crossings.

lines.text: Turn, lane, one-way and speed rules.

narration.text: To finish, at a stop sign, stop completely and yield to traffic and pedestrians before going on. At a yield sign, slow down and let vehicles crossing your path go first. Roundabout Ahead, Stop Ahead and Yield Ahead signs warn you early. No Turn On Red forbids turning on a red light, and other signs ban right turns or U-turns. Lane-use signs show which lanes may turn, and a Center Lane Left Turn Only sign reserves the middle lane. A One Way sign means every lane moves the same direction, and a speed limit sign sets the legal maximum. The hook is full stop, then yield.

why_how.text: Some signs exist to keep you out of places you must never drive, so they need an immediate response.
Freeway crossovers are for responders, so other drivers turn around by exiting and re-entering.
Keep Left and obstacle signs both guide you around something in the road, but in different ways.

scenario.text: After missing an exit, Kim sees a freeway crossover marked Authorized Vehicles Only.

reasoning.text: The crossover is reserved for police, emergency or maintenance vehicles; to reverse direction, exit and re-enter the freeway the other way.

result.text: Kim drives to the next exit, leaves the freeway, and re-enters going the other way.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Wrong Way and Do Not Enter mean the same thing.

correction.text: Wrong Way means you are already in an oncoming lane, while Do Not Enter forbids going into the area in the first place.

prompt.text: A sign ahead shows a traffic island and says you may pass it on either side. Which sign is it, and what may you do?

answer.text: An Obstacle in Roadway sign; you may pass on either side.

rationale.text: An Obstacle in Roadway sign means an island or obstruction is ahead and you may pass on either side, unlike Keep Left.

narration.text: This lesson covers signs that keep you out of places and guide you around things in the road. Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs protect you from driving against traffic. Authorized Vehicles Only signs mark freeway crossovers that only responders may use. No Trucks signs bar trucks from certain areas. And Keep Left and Obstacle in Roadway signs tell you how to get past an island or obstruction. Some of these signs call for an instant response, so it pays to know them well. Practice questions often pair two of them and ask which applies, so we will compare them side by side.

title.text: Do Not Enter and Wrong Way

lines.text: Do Not Enter: you may not drive in.
Wrong Way: you are in oncoming traffic.

narration.text: A Do Not Enter sign means you may not drive into that area. It is posted at places like the wrong end of a one-way street or a freeway exit ramp. A Wrong Way sign means you have already entered a lane of oncoming traffic and must get out as quickly and safely as possible. So the two signs come in order. Do Not Enter tries to stop you before you go in. Wrong Way tells you that you already did. If you see a Wrong Way sign, slow down, pull over safely when you can, and turn around. Every second in an oncoming lane is a serious risk.

lines.text: To turn around: exit and re-enter.

narration.text: Authorized Vehicles Only marks a freeway emergency crossover reserved for police, emergency or maintenance vehicles. These gaps in the median let responders turn around quickly. They are not for other drivers, even if you missed your exit. To reverse direction, exit and re-enter the freeway the other way. A No Trucks sign bars trucks from the posted area. These two signs are both about who may use a road or space. The crossover sign limits use to authorized vehicles, and the No Trucks sign keeps one kind of vehicle out. Either way, the rule is set by the sign.

lines.text: Keep Left: go left of the feature.

narration.text: A Keep Left sign means traffic should go only to the left of a road feature or obstruction, such as a median or a traffic island. An Obstacle in Roadway sign means a traffic island or obstruction is ahead and you may pass on either side. So both signs warn you about something in the road, but they give different instructions. Keep Left gives you one choice: the left side. The obstacle sign gives you two: left or right. The difference matters because going right of a Keep Left feature can put you into oncoming traffic or onto a curb.

title.text: Wrong Way or Do Not Enter

lines.text: Trap: the two signs are the same.
Wrong Way: you are already in.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Wrong Way means you are already in an oncoming lane, while Do Not Enter forbids going into the area in the first place. Options may say the two signs mean the same thing, or swap them, claiming Do Not Enter means you are already in the wrong lane. Both are wrong. Do Not Enter is a warning at the entrance. Wrong Way is an alarm after the entrance. The action also differs. At Do Not Enter, you simply do not go in. At Wrong Way, you must get out as quickly and safely as possible. Knowing which one you passed tells you what to do next.

Here is a quick check: a sign ahead shows a traffic island, and it tells you that you may pass on either side. Which sign is it, and what may you do? Recall the two island signs. An Obstacle in Roadway sign means a traffic island or obstruction is ahead and you may pass on either side. A Keep Left sign means go only to the left. Since this sign allows either side, it is the Obstacle in Roadway sign, and you may pass on the left or the right. If it had been a Keep Left sign, only the left side would have been allowed.

To finish, a Do Not Enter sign means you may not drive into that area, and a Wrong Way sign means you have entered a lane of oncoming traffic and must get out as quickly and safely as possible. Authorized Vehicles Only marks a freeway crossover reserved for police, emergency or maintenance vehicles, so to reverse direction you exit and re-enter the freeway the other way. A No Trucks sign bars trucks from the area. A Keep Left sign means go only to the left of a feature, while an Obstacle in Roadway sign means you may pass on either side. The hook is wrong way, get out.

why_how.text: No-passing zones mark places where passing would be hazardous, so signs mark where they start and end.
The orange triangle warns that a vehicle ahead travels slowly, so you can adjust in time.
Railroad advance signs and crossbucks warn of tracks ahead, including crossings with several tracks.

scenario.text: On a country road, Eve comes up behind a farm combine with an orange triangle on its back.

reasoning.text: The orange triangle marks vehicles that do not travel faster than twenty-five miles per hour, so drive with care around them.

result.text: Eve slows, keeps a safe distance, and passes only where passing is allowed and safe.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the Pass With Care sign starts a no-passing zone.

correction.text: Do Not Pass forbids passing, and Pass With Care, posted on the right after it, ends the no-passing zone.

prompt.text: You see a yellow pennant on the left side of the road. What is it warning you about?

answer.text: A no-passing zone, where passing would be hazardous.

rationale.text: The yellow No Passing Zone pennant sits on the left side and warns that passing would be hazardous.

narration.text: This lesson covers signs about passing, slow vehicles and railroad crossings ahead. Passing is one of the riskiest moves on a two-lane road, so signs tell you where it is forbidden and where it is allowed again. We will look at Do Not Pass and Pass With Care signs, the yellow pennant on the left side of the road, the orange triangle on slow vehicles, and the RR and crossbuck signs that warn of tracks. Practice questions often test which passing sign starts a zone and which one ends it, so we will keep the order of those signs clear.

lines.text: Pass With Care: the zone ends.

narration.text: A Do Not Pass sign prohibits passing. A Pass With Care sign, posted on the right, marks the end of that no-passing zone, so you may pass when safe. The yellow No Passing Zone pennant sits on the left side of the road and warns that passing would be hazardous. So the pennant and the Do Not Pass sign both tell you a no-passing zone is here, while Pass With Care tells you it is over. Passing when safe still means checking for oncoming traffic, hills and curves. The end of the zone is permission to consider passing, not a command to pass.

The orange slow-moving vehicle triangle is mounted on the back of vehicles that do not travel faster than twenty-five miles per hour, such as Amish buggies and farm combines. Drive with care around them, because you will close on them quickly. A sign marked RR warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. The railroad crossbuck in the handbook's sign challenge warns that a crossing made up of three tracks is ahead. So railroad signs tell you both that a crossing is coming and, sometimes, how many tracks it has. More tracks mean more places a train could appear, so look along every one.

lines.text: Trap: Pass With Care starts the zone.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Do Not Pass and Pass With Care work as a pair: the first forbids passing, and the second, posted on the right after it, ends the no-passing zone. Options may reverse them, or say both signs forbid passing. Both are wrong. The word care in Pass With Care can make it sound like a warning not to pass, but it is the sign that ends the zone. Another trap is the side of the road. The pennant is on the left, while Pass With Care is on the right. When a question names a side, use it as a clue to which sign is meant.

lines.text: On the left side of the road.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a two-lane road, you see a yellow pennant-shaped sign on the left side of the road. What is it warning you about? Recall the passing signs. The yellow No Passing Zone pennant sits on the left side of the road and warns that passing would be hazardous. So the answer is a no-passing zone. Stay in your lane and do not start a pass until a Pass With Care sign on the right marks the end of the zone and it is safe. The pennant's position on the left puts it right in your line of sight as you consider pulling out.

To finish, a Do Not Pass sign prohibits passing, and a Pass With Care sign on the right marks the end of that zone, so you may pass when safe. The yellow No Passing Zone pennant sits on the left side of the road and warns that passing would be hazardous. The orange slow-moving vehicle triangle marks vehicles that do not travel faster than twenty-five miles per hour, such as Amish buggies and farm combines, so drive with care. A sign marked RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead, and a crossbuck can show a crossing with several tracks. The hook is one starts, one ends.

why_how.text: Warning signs give you time to slow down before a hazard instead of reacting at the last second.
Some warnings point to people nearby, such as children, bicyclists, pedestrians and road crews.
Bridges can ice before the road, so a bridge can be slick while the road looks fine.

scenario.text: Ben approaches a curve with a Winding Curve Ahead sign and a speed plaque below it.

reasoning.text: A Winding Curve Ahead sign with a speed plaque tells you to limit your speed, in the handbook example to thirty-five miles per hour.

result.text: Ben slows to the plaque speed before entering the curves.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a clear road means the bridge ahead is clear too.

correction.text: Bridge Ices Before Road warns that a bridge may be icy even when the road is clear.

prompt.text: A Hill sign warns of a steep downgrade ahead. What should every driver do?

answer.text: Check the brakes and gear down if needed.

rationale.text: A Hill sign warns of a steep downgrade, so every vehicle, especially a large truck, should check brakes and gear down if needed.

lines.text: People on and near the road.

narration.text: This lesson covers warning signs, the yellow and orange signs that tell you about something ahead before you reach it. Some warn about the road itself: curves, hills, slippery surfaces and bridges that ice. Some warn about people: children, bicyclists, pedestrians and road crews. Others give a number to respect, such as a clearance height or an exit speed. And some warn of roads joining yours. The purpose of every warning sign is the same: to give you time to slow down and prepare. Practice questions usually describe one sign and ask what it means or what to do.

lines.text: Road Turns Left: one sharp turn.
Road Curves Ahead: left, then right.

narration.text: A Road Turns Left sign warns of a sharp turn or curve to the left. A Road Curves Ahead sign warns of a sharp curve to the left and then to the right. A Winding Curve Ahead sign with a speed plaque tells you to limit your speed, in the handbook example to thirty-five miles per hour. An Intersection Ahead sign warns of a crossing road, while a Side Road Ahead sign warns of a road joining from the right. So read the arrow on the sign. It shows the shape of the road ahead, and it tells you whether another road crosses yours or simply joins from one side.

lines.text: Check brakes; gear down if needed.
Slippery when wet; bridges ice first.

narration.text: A Hill sign warns of a steep downgrade. Every vehicle, especially a large truck, should check its brakes and gear down if needed, so the brakes do not overheat on the way down. Slippery When Wet warns that the road surface becomes slick in bad weather. Bridge Ices Before Road warns that a bridge may be icy even when the road is clear. Bridges lose heat from above and below, so they freeze sooner than the road leading to them. Each of these signs asks you to slow down before the hazard, because braking hard on a slick surface or a steep grade is where trouble starts.

A School Children Present sign means children are nearby, so drive carefully and follow a school crossing guard's directions. Watch for Bicyclists and Watch for Pedestrians signs mean those road users may be nearby, so drive carefully. A Bicyclists and Pedestrians sign marks a nearby shared crossing for both groups. The orange Road Work Ahead sign means crews are working in the area, so drive with care. These signs all point to people who are outside a car and easy to hurt. Slow down, look wider, and be ready to stop for anyone stepping into the road.

lines.text: Maximum Height: clearance under a structure.
Exit speed: no faster than posted.

narration.text: A Maximum Height sign gives the clearance under a bridge or structure, such as twelve feet six inches. That matters most if you drive a tall vehicle or carry a load on the roof. An exit speed sign, such as one posted at twenty-five miles per hour, means you should take the exit at no more than that speed. Exit ramps often curve tightly, and the speed on the sign is set for that curve. Both signs give you a number to plan around before you reach the place itself. Check your vehicle's height before you need it, and start slowing for the exit while you are still on the main road.

title.text: A clear road, an icy bridge

lines.text: Trap: clear road means clear bridge.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Bridge Ices Before Road warns that a bridge may be icy even when the road is clear. Many drivers judge the bridge by the road they are on, and that is the mistake. Options may say the sign means the bridge is closed, or that the road is icier than the bridge. Both are wrong. The bridge freezes first. A related sign, Slippery When Wet, warns that the road surface becomes slick in bad weather. When you see either sign in cold or wet weather, slow down before you reach the slick spot, and avoid sudden braking or steering on it.

Here is a quick check: a Hill sign warns of a steep downgrade ahead. What should every driver do? Recall the Hill sign. A Hill sign warns of a steep downgrade, and every vehicle, especially a large truck, should check its brakes and gear down if needed. So the answer is to check your brakes and shift to a lower gear if needed before you start down. A lower gear helps hold the vehicle's speed, so the brakes do not have to do all the work and overheat. Speeding up to build momentum, or coasting in neutral, would be exactly the wrong choice.

lines.text: Read the arrow; slow for curves.

narration.text: To finish, Road Turns Left warns of one sharp left turn, Road Curves Ahead warns of a curve left and then right, and a speed plaque under Winding Curve Ahead tells you to limit your speed. Intersection Ahead warns of a crossing road, and Side Road Ahead warns of one joining from the right. A Hill sign means check brakes and gear down. Slippery When Wet and Bridge Ices Before Road warn of slick surfaces. School, bicyclist, pedestrian and Road Work Ahead signs mean people are near. Maximum Height gives clearance, and an exit speed sign is the most you should drive. The hook is bridges freeze first.

why_how.text: Merge and lane-end signs give you time to adjust before lanes join or disappear.
When a divided highway ends, traffic in the other direction is no longer separated, so you keep right.
Pavement markings warn, regulate and inform, so each line color and pattern has a meaning.

scenario.text: Ana drives in the right lane and sees Right Lane Ends, then Lane Ends Merge Left.

reasoning.text: The right lane is ending, so merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane.

result.text: Ana signals, finds a gap, yields, and merges left before her lane ends.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers in the left lane must make room when your lane ends.

correction.text: A Lane Ends Merge Left sign means you merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane.

prompt.text: You are driving on a road with two lanes going your way, separated by a broken white line. What may you never do with that line?

rationale.text: Never straddle a broken white line or cross a double yellow line.

narration.text: This lesson covers signs about lanes joining, ending and changing, and the basics of pavement markings. When lanes merge or disappear, drivers who are not ready make sudden moves, so signs give early notice. We will look at Merging Traffic, Lane Ends Merge Left, Right Lane Ends, Divided Highway Ends and Two-Way Traffic signs. Then we will turn to the lines on the road: what colors they come in, what they do, and which ones you must never straddle or cross. Practice questions often ask who yields when a lane ends, so we will make that point especially clear.

lines.text: Merging Traffic: joins from the right.
Right Lane Ends: merge left soon.

narration.text: A Merging Traffic sign means traffic will merge from the right, so watch for vehicles joining your road and be ready to adjust. A Right Lane Ends sign gives notice that the right lane ends in five hundred feet, so prepare to merge left. A Lane Ends Merge Left sign means the right lane is ending, so merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane. Notice who does what. With Merging Traffic, others join you. With Lane Ends, you are the one who must move, and you are the one who yields. Signal early, find a gap, and merge smoothly.

lines.text: Divided Highway Ends: two lanes of traffic.

narration.text: A Divided Highway Ends sign means the divided road becomes two lanes of traffic, one in each direction. A Two-Way Traffic sign means two-way traffic begins, so keep right. These signs matter because the median or barrier that kept oncoming traffic away is about to disappear. On the divided road, you may have been driving in either lane. Now, the lane to your left belongs to drivers coming toward you. Move right, stay right, and watch for oncoming vehicles. Passing on the new two-way road follows the ordinary rules, so look for markings and signs before you consider it.

Pavement markings are white or yellow, and they warn, regulate and inform drivers. White lines divide lanes of traffic moving in the same direction. Broken white lines separate lanes on roads with more than one lane moving the same way. And two rules about lines are firm: never straddle a broken white line, and never cross a double yellow line. Straddling a lane line means driving with the line under the middle of your car, which leaves drivers on both sides unsure of where you are. Choose a lane and stay centered in it, so everyone around you knows which lane is yours.

title.text: Who yields at a lane end

lines.text: Trap: left-lane drivers must let you in.
Your lane ends, so you merge.
You yield to the left lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A Lane Ends Merge Left sign means the right lane is ending, so merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane. Options may suggest that drivers in the left lane must slow down to make room, or that the merging driver has the right of way. Both are wrong. The driver whose lane ends is the one who adjusts. Compare the Merging Traffic sign, which warns that others will merge from the right into your road. Same idea, different side. In either case, the driver entering the lane is the one who yields to traffic already in it.

lines.text: A broken white line between them.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving on a road with two lanes going your way, separated by a broken white line. What may you never do with that line? Recall the line rules. Broken white lines separate lanes on roads with more than one lane moving the same way, and you must never straddle a broken white line or cross a double yellow line. So the answer is that you may never straddle it. Pick one lane and stay centered in it. Riding along on top of the line leaves drivers in both lanes unsure of where you are going.

To finish, a Merging Traffic sign means traffic will merge from the right. A Right Lane Ends sign gives notice that the right lane ends in five hundred feet, and a Lane Ends Merge Left sign means you merge left and yield to traffic already in that lane. A Divided Highway Ends sign means the road becomes two lanes of traffic, and a Two-Way Traffic sign means two-way traffic begins, so keep right. Pavement markings are white or yellow and warn, regulate and inform. White lines divide same-direction lanes, and you never straddle a broken white line or cross a double yellow line. The hook is merge left and yield.
